subject: Posterior predictive density with latent variables in STAN

messages.author: e151edd4c9d2f4c8
messages.subject: Posterior predictive density with latent variables in STAN
parts:
This is essentially a repost of this post on statexchange:
http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/206637/posterior-predictive-density-with-latent-variables-in-stan

Using STAN, how do one calculate the posterior predictive density in a model with latent variables in a specified point.

As an example consider a model with a single random effect:

Y_ij = a*delta_i + b*epsilon_ij     i=1,...,N,    j=1,...,K

where delta_i is N(0,1) and epsilon_ij is N(0,1). The model has two parameters theta=(a,b). We can build the model in STAN with flat priors

-------- STAN model ----------
data {
  int N;
  int K;
  real y[N,K];
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> a;
  real<lower=0> b;
  real delta[N];
}

model {
  for ( n in 1:N){
    delta[n] ~ normal(0, a);
    y[n] ~ normal(delta[n], b);
  }
}
-----------------------------------------

Now given a new data point Y = (Y_1,...,Y_K), we want to compute the posterior predictive density

p_post(Y) =  \int p(y | theta) p_post(theta)  d theta

We could use the "generated quantities" block in STAN and compute P(Y|a,b), this however requires us to integrate out delta, i.e.

p(Y|a,b) = \int p(Y|a,b,delta)p(delta|a,b) d\delta

For this particular model this integration yields a closed-form expression, but for more complex models this is not the case.

Is there some general scheme that can be exploited in the STAN framework to obtain this posterior density? I have considered numerical integration but I think that it will require a large amount of model specific effort. Naive Monte Carlo integration can easily fail if p(Y|a,b,delta) is large in regions where p(\delta|a,b) is small.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior predictive density with latent variables in STAN
parts:
I hadn't thought about this before, so somebody who's better at
importance sampling and integration than me should check my second
answer.

You can either draw the random delta in the generated quantities,
which can be problematic if the prior on delta_tilde_n doesn't have
much mass near y_tilde[n]:

data {
int<lower=0> N_tilde;
real y_tilde[N_tilde];
...

generated quantities {
real log_p_y_tilde[N_tilde];
for (n in 1:N_tilde) {
real delta_tilde_n;
delta_tilde_n <- normal_rng(0, a);
log_p_y_tilde[n] <- normal_log(y_tilde[n], delta_tilde_n, b);
}
}

Alternatively, you can declare delta_tilde as a parameter, then
evaluate log densities on draws from the posterior, which can
then be importance weighted into an estimate of log p(y_tilde | a, b).

parameters {
real delta_tilde[N_tilde];

model {
delta_tilde ~ normal(0, a);
y_tilde ~ normal(delta_tilde, b);

generated quantities {
real log_p_y_tilde[N_tilde];
real weight[N_tilde];
for (n in 1:N_tilde) {
log_weight[n] <- log_normal(delta_tilde[n], 0, a);
log_p_y_tilde[n] <- normal_log(y_tilde[n], delta_tilde[n], b);
}

You'll need to use the log weights from the outside of Stan (because
it involves multiple draw calculations), to create the appropriate
importance weighted expectation.

This can also lead to a kind of semi-supervised learning in some
cases where adding delta_tilde and y_tilde to the model inform the estimates
of parameters. I don't think that happens here.

In both cases, you have to be careful, because the average of logs
isn't the same as the log of the average, and we usually want the latter.
That requires some further log-sum-exp gymnastics, as I outline in the
case study section "Calculating posterior log density":

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/pool-binary-trials.html

- Bob

PS. "Stan" is not an acronym.

messages.author: e151edd4c9d2f4c8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior predictive density with latent variables in STAN
parts:
Thank you for the excellent answer. The importance sampling idea was exactly the kind of thing I was hoping for - using Stan's MCMC sampler to get at values of delta where P(Y|a,b,delta)*P(delta|a,b) is large. However I am worried about spill-over of information causing, as you say, a kind of semi-supervised learning scenario. This will definitely be a problem for the model from which I derived this example - I believe it is a problem even for the example model. I have included code to show this:

---------- Stan Model ----------
data {
  int<lower=0> N;

}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> a;
  real<lower=0> b;
  real delta[N];

delta[n] ~ normal(0, a);
    y[n] ~ normal(delta[n], b);
  }

for(n in 1:N_tilde){
    delta_tilde[n] ~ normal(0, a);
    y_tilde[n] ~ normal(delta_tilde[n], b);

--------------------------------

-------------- R ---------------
# Test calculation of posterior predictive in mixed effect model
N <- 50
K <- 5
a <- 4
b <- 2

N_tilde <- 50 # N_tilde <- 0
a_tilde <- 12
b_tilde <- 2

y <- matrix( a*rnorm(N)+b*rnorm(N*K), N, K)
y_tilde <- matrix( a_tilde*rnorm(N_tilde)+b_tilde*rnorm(N*K), N_tilde, K)

library(rstan)
stan_mixed <- stan_model("stan/test/post_lik.stan")

stan_fit <- sampling(stan_mixed)
# With N_tilde = 0 result in a posterior mean around the true value 4
# With N_tilde = 50 the posterior mean is around 9
stan_hist(stan_fit, pars=c('a'))
----------------------------------

There seem to be a conflict in wanting to sample delta_tilde without it affecting the likelihood of the model.

One more thing: The calculation of the importance sampling weight. We are to evaluate
  p(Y_tilde|a,b) = \int p(Y_tilde|a,b,delta_tilde)p(delta_tilde|a,b) d delta_tilde
for a fixed theta=(a,b). We do importance sampling so instead of sampling from p(delta_tilde|a,b), we sample from "p_post(delta_tilde)". The log importance sampling weight would be:

log p(delta_tilde|a,b) - log p_post(delta_tilde).

I can see the term log p(delta_tilde|a,b) = normal_log(delta_tilde, 0, a), but where is -log p_post(delta_tilde). Am I missing something here.

Thanks again,
Tobias
